salts.name: Barium chloride solution, 0.1 M

leftOut.value: BaO, a molecule of one barium atom and one oxygen atom, gives bands between 450 nm and 790 nm that are strong in the flame too. They are spread over most of the scale, and the strip leaves them out.
BaCl, a molecule of one barium atom and one chlorine atom, gives narrow bands near 514 nm and 524 nm, inside the broad green band. The strip leaves them out.

notes.value: Most of the light of this flame comes from a molecule and not from barium atoms. The molecule is BaOH: one barium atom, one oxygen atom and one hydrogen atom, joined in the flame. It gives the broad green band from about 480 nm to 550 nm.
The barium atom gives the sharp green line near 553.5 nm, beside the band.
That is why the flame is not the colour of the lines on barium's card of the periodic table. The card shows lines of the barium atom alone, and the flame's green is mostly the molecule's.

salts.classifiedAs: Hazards of solid barium chloride dihydrate, the pure substance, from a supplier's safety data sheet

note.value: The solution on this bench is 0.1 mol/L, which is about 2% barium chloride by mass (worked out from the molarity, not read from a source). The same supplier's sheet for barium chloride solutions of less than 1 M, which covers this strength, gives the signal word Warning and one statement, under the codes H303 and H333: the solution may be harmful if it is swallowed or breathed in. In its section on toxicology the same sheet still calls barium chloride highly toxic, and names the heart, the nerves and the kidneys among the organs it harms. The sheet calls for eye protection, gloves and protective clothing. It says that a splash in the eyes is to be rinsed with water for several minutes, with contact lenses taken out if that is easily done, and the rinsing then kept up, and that a splash on the skin is to be washed off with plenty of water. If the solution is swallowed, it says, the mouth is to be rinsed, and a poison centre or a doctor called if the person feels unwell. Three other documents are stricter, and this lab goes by the stricter. A second supplier's sheet for a 0.1 M solution of barium chloride has a graver statement for swallowing: under H302, the solution is harmful if swallowed, where the first sheet says that it may be; for breathing it in, it has the same H333. That sheet says that the mist, the vapour or the spray of the solution is not to be breathed, and that nobody is to eat, drink or smoke while using it. For the eyes it asks for flushing with water for 15 minutes or more, with contact lenses out and the eyelids lifted now and then, and for a doctor at once; for the skin, for wet clothing to come off and the skin to be washed with mild soap and water; and, if any is swallowed, for a doctor or a poison centre to be called at once. A third supplier's sheet, for the solid, adds a statement that the first supplier's sheet for the solid does not have: that the substance seriously irritates the eyes. NOAA's CAMEO Chemicals record of the solid asks for the longest rinse of the eyes, 20 to 30 minutes, with a hospital or a poison centre called meanwhile and the person then taken to hospital. As to what becomes of the solution afterwards, the second supplier's sheet says that a spill is to be kept out of storm drains and out of ditches that run to a waterway, the third supplier's says that the substance should not get out into the environment, and NOAA's record shows barium compounds on the consolidated list of regulated chemicals of the United States Environmental Protection Agency. How any of it is disposed of is decided by the laboratory's own rules and by local regulations; ask the laboratory's supervisor.

salts.name: Calcium chloride solution, 0.1 M

leftOut.value: CaOH also gives weaker bands on either side of the orange-red one, brightest near 603 nm and 643 nm. The strip leaves them out.

notes.value: Most of the light of this flame comes from a molecule and not from calcium atoms. The molecule is CaOH: one calcium atom, one oxygen atom and one hydrogen atom, joined in the flame. It gives both broad bands: the orange-red one from about 614 nm to 640 nm, which is the brighter, and the green one from about 540 nm to 568 nm.
The calcium atom gives the sharp violet line near 422.7 nm.
That is why the flame is not the colour of the lines on calcium's card of the periodic table. The card shows lines of the calcium atom alone, and the flame's orange-red is mostly the molecule's.

salts.classifiedAs: Hazards of solid calcium chloride (anhydrous), the pure substance, from a supplier's safety data sheet

note.value: The solution on this bench is 0.1 mol/L, which is about 1.1% calcium chloride by mass (worked out from the molarity, not read from a source). The same supplier has one sheet for calcium chloride solution, with no strength in its title; its table of composition takes in solutions of 1% to 15% of the dihydrate, and this one, at about 1.5% counted so, is inside that range. The sheet prints no signal word and no hazard statement: it says that its solution is not classed as hazardous, and that every laboratory chemical is to be treated with caution all the same. It calls for eye protection, gloves and protective clothing. It says that a splash in the eyes is to be rinsed with water for several minutes, with contact lenses taken out if that is easily done, and the rinsing then kept up, and that a splash on the skin is to be washed off with plenty of water. Three other documents are stricter, and this lab goes by the stricter. A second supplier's sheet for a 0.1 M solution of calcium chloride gives the signal word Warning and one statement, under H320: the solution irritates the eyes. For the eyes it asks for flushing with water for 15 minutes or more, with contact lenses out and the eyelids lifted now and then, and for a doctor at once; for the skin, for wet clothing to come off and the skin to be washed with mild soap and water, and for a doctor if it becomes irritated. NOAA's CAMEO Chemicals record of the solid also asks for 15 minutes or more for the eyes, and for an eye doctor to be consulted. A third supplier's sheet, for the solid, lists one hazard that the first supplier's sheet for the solid does not, and it is of the dry solid only: that its dust may form a mixture with air that can burn. The same sheet says elsewhere that calcium chloride is not combustible. As to what becomes of the solution afterwards, the second supplier's sheet says that a spill is to be kept out of storm drains and out of ditches that run to a waterway, and the third supplier's says that the substance should not get out into the environment. How any of it is disposed of is decided by the laboratory's own rules and by local regulations; ask the laboratory's supervisor.

salts.name: Copper(II) chloride solution, 0.1 M

leftOut.value: Copper oxide gives two bands in the red. The source read for this lab does not say where they are, so the strip does not show them.

notes.value: Most of the light of this flame comes from molecules and not from copper atoms. CuCl, one copper atom joined to one chlorine atom, gives the blue band from about 400 nm to 470 nm. CuOH, one copper atom joined to one oxygen atom and one hydrogen atom, gives the green band near 550 nm. The flame's blue-green is the two together.
No line of the copper atom is on the strip: the sources read for this lab give none between 400 nm and 780 nm for a flame.
That is why the flame is not the colour of the lines on copper's card of the periodic table. The card shows lines of the copper atom alone, and the flame's blue-green is the molecules'.

salts.classifiedAs: Hazards of solid copper(II) chloride dihydrate, the pure substance, from a supplier's safety data sheet

statements: H314: Causes severe skin burns and eye damage

note.value: The solution on this bench is 0.1 mol/L, which is about 1.3% copper(II) chloride by mass (worked out from the molarity, not read from a source). The same supplier's sheet for copper(II) chloride solutions of less than 0.99 M, which covers this strength, gives the signal word Warning and two statements: under H303, that the solution may be harmful if swallowed; and under H315 and H319, that it irritates the skin and seriously irritates the eyes. The sheet calls for eye protection, gloves and protective clothing. It says that a splash in the eyes is to be rinsed with water for several minutes, with contact lenses taken out if that is easily done, and the rinsing then kept up, that a splash on the skin is to be washed off with plenty of water, and that medical advice is to be sought if the skin becomes irritated. If the solution is swallowed, it says, the mouth is to be rinsed, and a poison centre or a doctor called if the person feels unwell. On what the solution does to living things in water, the sheet says only that it has no data yet. Three other documents are stricter, and this lab goes by the stricter. A second supplier's sheet for a 0.1 M solution of copper(II) chloride has a graver statement for swallowing (under H302, harmful if swallowed), the same two for the skin and the eyes (H315 and H319), and one that the first sheet does not have: under H410, that the solution is very toxic to life in water, with effects that last a long time. It says that nobody is to eat, drink or smoke while using the solution. For the eyes it asks for flushing with water for 15 minutes or more, with contact lenses out and the eyelids lifted now and then, and for a doctor at once; for the skin, for wet clothing to come off and the skin to be washed with mild soap and water. A third supplier's sheet, for the solid, says the same of life in water, and adds that the substance is harmful in contact with the skin. NOAA's CAMEO Chemicals record of copper chloride says that its solutions irritate the eyes and asks for 15 minutes of flushing. As to what becomes of the solution afterwards, all three say that it is to be kept out of sewers and waterways, and the third supplier's sheet says out of drains as well; the two suppliers' sheets add that it is not to be let out into the environment, and the second supplier's that what is spilt is to be collected. NOAA's record shows copper compounds, and this chloride by name, on the consolidated list of regulated chemicals of the United States Environmental Protection Agency. How any of it is disposed of is decided by the laboratory's own rules and by local regulations; ask the laboratory's supervisor.

salts.name: Potassium chloride solution, 0.1 M

leftOut.value: A potassium flame also gives a faint glow spread along the scale, with no lines in it. The strip leaves it out.

notes.value: The light of this flame comes from potassium atoms. They give a pair of lines in the deep red, near 766.5 nm and 769.9 nm, and a fainter pair in the violet, near 404.4 nm and 404.7 nm. Each pair is too close together for a hand spectroscope to separate, so each is seen as one line.
The deep red pair lies beyond 700 nm, about where the eye stops seeing. On a real bench it looks faint however strong it is, and a potassium flame can be hard to see.
Here the flame's colour is the atom's own. Potassium's card on the periodic table shows the violet pair and not the deep red one, because the card stops at 700 nm.

salts.classifiedAs: Hazards of solid potassium chloride, the pure substance, from a supplier's safety data sheet

statements: H303: May be harmful if swallowed

note.value: The solution on this bench is 0.1 mol/L, which is about 0.7% potassium chloride by mass (worked out from the molarity, not read from a source). The same supplier has one sheet for potassium chloride solution, with no strength in its title; its table of composition runs from 1% to 4% potassium chloride, so this solution is a little weaker than any the table lists, and the supplier has no sheet for it. This note rests on that sheet, the nearest one for a stronger solution. The sheet prints no signal word and no hazard statement: it says that its solution is not classed as hazardous, and that every laboratory chemical is to be treated with caution all the same. It calls for eye protection, gloves and protective clothing. It says that a splash in the eyes is to be rinsed with water for several minutes, with contact lenses taken out if that is easily done, and the rinsing then kept up, and that a splash on the skin is to be washed off with plenty of water. Two other documents, both about the solid, ask for more after a splash, and this lab goes by the stricter. A second supplier's sheet does not class the solid as hazardous, where the first supplier's sheet for the solid has the statement above; but it asks for rinsing of the eyes for 15 minutes or more, under the eyelids too, with a doctor seen, and for 15 minutes or more of washing for the skin. NOAA's CAMEO Chemicals record asks for the longest rinse of the eyes, 20 to 30 minutes, with a hospital or a poison centre called meanwhile and the person then taken to hospital, and for the skin to be flooded with water while wet clothing comes off; it says that large doses by mouth upset the gut and the heartbeat. As to what becomes of the solution afterwards, the second supplier's sheet says that the substance should not get out into the environment. How any of it is disposed of is decided by the laboratory's own rules and by local regulations; ask the laboratory's supervisor.

salts.name: Sodium chloride solution, 0.1 M

notes.value: The light of this flame comes from sodium atoms. They give two yellow lines, near 589.0 nm and 589.6 nm, too close together for a hand spectroscope to separate: it shows one sharp yellow line.
Here the flame's colour is the atom's own. Sodium's card on the periodic table shows the same two lines.
This yellow is strong enough that a little sodium hides the colour of another salt in the same flame, though a spectroscope still shows the other salt's light beside sodium's line.

It says that a splash in the eyes is to be rinsed with water for several minutes, with contact lenses taken out if that is easily done, and the rinsing then kept up, and that a splash on the skin is to be washed off with plenty of water. Two other suppliers' sheets, both for the solid, ask for more after a splash and in clearing up, and this lab goes by the stricter. handlingTraceShows.rationale: A loop that has been handled and not cleaned shows sodium in the flame and in the spectroscope as fully as a loop dipped in the sodium chloride solution does. A real trace from the fingers is far smaller: it gives a brief, fainter yellow, and some loops give none that can be seen. The model makes it this large so that a learner who skips the cleaning always sees what the skipped step costs. Whether a trace is there is from a source; how large it is here is the model's choice.

unresolvedWithinNm.rationale: Two lines of one salt closer together than this many nanometres are stored as one feature, the stronger line with its partner, and are seen as one sharp line. Sodium's two yellow lines are 0.6 nm apart, potassium's violet pair 0.3 nm and its deep red pair 3.4 nm. A hand spectroscope's scale is read to a few nanometres at best, and 5 nm is this lab's figure for it, not a measurement of any instrument. No two lines stored as separate features of one salt are closer than this.

approximateBandMarginNm.rationale: A band whose sources give only where it is brightest, and not where it ends, is drawn this many nanometres wider on each side than those positions, so that it reads as a band and not as a line. The width drawn is the picture's; it is not a measurement, and the band's callout says that its limits are not given.

ranges.rationale: The choices for where on the scale the brightest thing is. They cover the scale from 400 nm to 780 nm with no gap, and each boundary is placed at least 5 nm from the brightest feature of every salt as it is drawn, so that the brightest feature of each of the six lies plainly inside one range and a learner who reads the scale to a few nanometres chooses the same range. The boundaries are this lab's and mark nothing in the chemistry.

mixedFlame.rationale: What a flame is called when the loop carries more than one salt and none of them is sodium: by the colour of each salt on the loop, in the order they were dipped, with no one colour chosen over another. What such a flame really looks like depends on how much of each salt is on the loop, which the model does not hold. With sodium on the loop the flame is sodium's yellow alone, and that part is from a source. In the spectroscope every salt's lines and bands are shown as that salt alone gives them, and the model does not rank the light of one salt against the light of another.
